decisions.decision: V2-027 is the fixture half of M6 and nothing else. It completes, against hand-authored contract fixtures in internal/provider, the three adapters' shared build/parse/normalize path, a Provider account pool, a provider usage window, a circuit breaker and the provider-neutral handoff conversion. It proves none of M6's four completion conditions in the form the roadmap states them, because every one of them names either a real Provider CLI or a real Preview exercise. The evidence must say so in a table (see d16) and the phrase capability exercised is forbidden anywhere in this task's evidence, docs or code comments.
decisions.rationale: Measured facts fix the boundary. docs/operations/v2-task-dag.md section 5 assigns V2-027 the component provider with live必須 = 不要, and section 9 records that codex and opencode are installed with non-interactive modes but unauthenticated (codex login status returns Not logged in; opencode auth list returns 0 credentials), and that authentication uses the owner's subscription identity so no agent can perform it. Gate rule G3.3 states that unit, fake, stub and contract-test evidence satisfies no real-environment condition at any grade. So a task that cannot invoke a Provider cannot satisfy a condition that names one, and pretending otherwise is the exact failure mode the phrase ban exists to prevent: capability exercised is the wording of validation.md section 3, which is about a real Preview revision with a real Provider, and reusing it for a fixture matrix would launder a contract test into a live claim.

decisions.decision: The claude adapter's argv is not changed. ClaudeAdapter.Build already emits claude --print --output-format json --no-session-persistence with the Work Packet on stdin, and that argv is live-proven wire-compatible. Completing the claude adapter therefore means only two things: giving it the full nine-case fixture matrix it does not have, and making it participate in the pool, window, breaker and handoff seams. No flag is added, removed or reordered.
decisions.rationale: docs/operations/v2-task-dag.md section 9 records the argv as measured wire-compatible against CLI version 2.1.241, and ev-v2-017-provider-live-claude, ev-v2-063-provider-live-claude-refresh and ev-v2-075-provider-live-claude-rebind each drove nine subtests through that exact argv against the real CLI. Changing it would discard three live observations to gain nothing, and would guarantee a fourth is needed before any M6 gate can bind.

decisions.decision: The opencode adapter's argv is corrected to the measured non-interactive surface. Today OpenCodeAdapter.Build emits opencode run --pure --format json --dir <workspace>. Only run and --format json are measured; --pure and --dir are not attested anywhere in the repository. The implementer measures the flag surface with opencode --version and opencode run --help only -- never the run subcommand itself -- and keeps exactly the flags that help declares and that are required for non-interactive execution and structured JSON on stdout. Workspace pinning is not re-expressed as a flag: Invocation.WorkingDirectory already carries it and ProcessSupervisor is what sets the child's directory. If help declares no flag for a property the adapter needs, the implementer records the gap and escalates rather than inventing a flag.
decisions.rationale: docs/operations/v2-task-dag.md section 9 records exactly one measured non-interactive path for opencode, opencode run --format json, measured by the coordinator on 2026-08-25 against version 1.18.22. Two of the four flags currently in the tree are therefore claims with no measurement behind them, and an argv that names a flag the CLI does not accept fails at exec time with a usage error that the adapter would classify as a transport failure -- a wrong class for a wrong argv, which is the least debuggable outcome available. Reading --help consumes no Provider usage, needs no authentication, and produces no completion, so it stays inside the task's non_goal (do not consume real Provider usage outside fixture capture) while removing the unmeasured claim. Relying on WorkingDirectory rather than a directory flag is also the shape the confinement already assumes: internal/runner.NamespaceConfinement pins the writable mount at Workspace and ProcessSupervisor sets Dir, so a flag would be a second, weaker copy of a boundary the kernel already holds.

decisions.decision: codex is inside this task for exactly one thing -- the same argv-truthfulness correction as d3 -- and inside the shared fixture matrix as a third adapter value. Everything about codex that needs authentication (real success, real model error, real quota exhaustion, real cancel) is V2-028's. CodexAdapter today emits codex exec --json --ephemeral -C <workspace>; only exec is measured. The same help-only measurement rule as d3 applies, with the same escalate-rather-than-invent rule.
decisions.rationale: The outcome names claude and opencode, so codex is not a completion target. But leaving three unmeasured flags in CodexAdapter while removing two from OpenCodeAdapter would be selectively honest about the same class of defect in the same file, and codex is not the representative Provider that earned an exemption -- the representative Provider proven live in M3 is claude (component provider-live-claude), so codex's argv has never met a real CLI either. Correcting an unmeasured argv is subtraction, not completion: it removes a claim, adds no capability, and cannot consume a Provider invocation. Keeping codex as a third value in the shared matrix is separately required: M6 completion condition 2 is about a change to the shared adapter code being demonstrated across all three, and a matrix over two of three cannot show that a change to build() or parseFixture() reaches the third.

decisions.decision: Contract fixtures live in internal/provider/testdata/ as JSON files, not in contracts/fixtures/ and not under any new schema in contracts/schemas/. Each fixture's bytes are exactly the projected shape that Adapter.Parse accepts, never a real CLI response, and any field carrying model output text (output, result, summary) is either absent or the literal form sha256 followed by a colon and 64 lowercase hex digits. A sibling manifest, internal/provider/testdata/manifest.json, records per fixture: provider name, declared CLI version, shape_source, observed_at, reason, and the live exercise that owns its real-CLI confirmation.
decisions.rationale: Three measured reasons pick the location. contracts/fixtures/ holds exactly one valid and one invalid instance for each of the nineteen schemas in contracts/schemas/, a strict one-to-one layout with no schema for a Provider CLI response; adding one would mean adding a schema, and contracts/release-contract and contracts/schemas are both out of scope. Second, contracts/** is the roots of the contracts component, and the reverse closure of contracts is eleven components (api, application, contracts, control-plane, internal-contracts, reconciler, release, runner, store-firestore, store-memory, task-ledger), measured from ci/components.json; internal/provider/** is the roots of provider alone, whose reverse closure is six. Third, validation.md's Provider adapter contract tests section is a test-pyramid layer, not a directory: it asks for minimal, secret-free fixtures captured from the real CLI per Provider, and requires fixture updates to carry CLI version, observation time, reason for change, and the corresponding Preview exercise -- which is what the manifest is for. The projected shape is not a convention this task invents: internal/runner/costledger_test.go TestClaudeAdapterParseRejectsRealShapeButProjectionSucceeds measures that ClaudeAdapter.Parse rejects the real claude CLI JSON outright (the decoder disallows unknown fields) and accepts only the projection whose output field is a digest, and internal/runner.projectRealCLIResult builds that projection in memory and drops the raw bytes. Writing a real response into a tracked file would be the one thing that construction exists to prevent.

decisions.decision: No fixture in this task is derived from any real CLI response. Every fixture is hand-authored to the projected shape and its manifest entry declares shape_source as projected-shape-hand-authored, with the reason naming this task and the corresponding_live_exercise naming provider-live-multi (V2-028). The manifest's declared CLI version is the version recorded in docs/operations/v2-task-dag.md section 9 for that Provider (claude 2.1.241, codex-cli 0.149.1, opencode 1.18.22), re-measured with --version by the implementer, and is labelled as the version the fixture is authored against, not the version a response was captured from.
decisions.rationale: Two of the three CLIs cannot produce a response at all, so a captured fixture set for all three is not obtainable in this task, and a set captured for claude alone would make the claude row structurally different from the other two in the one matrix whose whole purpose is that the three rows are the same. Declaring hand-authored provenance honestly is also the only form that survives V2-028: when the real responses exist, V2-028 replaces a declared shape with a measured one and the manifest diff shows exactly that. The alternative -- writing captured claude bytes now -- would consume Provider usage this task's non_goals forbid outside fixture capture, and would land a real response in a tracked file against d5.

decisions.decision: The fixture matrix is validation.md's nine cases, taken verbatim, applied to all three adapters: success; explicit model error; quota or usage exhaustion; non-zero exit; zero exit with an error envelope; empty or malformed structured output; timeout or cancel; usage obtainable and usage not obtainable (two rows); and CLI version incompatibility. Timeout and cancel are exercised through ClassifyError and NormalizeError rather than through a fixture file, because they are conditions of the invocation and not shapes of an output. Every other case is a file, run through the same table for all three adapters, with the expected Result including its FailureClass, Retryable and Ambiguous values asserted per cell.
decisions.rationale: The list is not invented here: docs/architecture/validation.md's Provider adapter contract tests section enumerates exactly these, and taking it verbatim is what makes the matrix auditable against the document instead of against the implementer's judgement. Running one table over three adapter values, rather than three tables, is what makes a change to the shared build() or parseFixture() code visibly reach all three -- the mechanism M6 completion condition 2 asks about. Splitting usage obtainable from usage not obtainable matters because Result.Usage zero is currently indistinguishable from usage absent, and the pool's window (d9) must not treat an unreported usage as zero consumption.

decisions.decision: The Provider account pool is a closed, three-slot registry in internal/provider keyed by adapter name, with exactly one slot per Provider. A slot holds: the name; whether the owner's standing authorization covers it; whether the Loop has ever completed an invocation through it; the id of the approved provider-preflight record that governs it, as a name only; a cooldown deadline; a consecutive-failure counter; the last observed failure class; and a slot state from a closed set (available, in-use, cooling-down, unauthenticated, quarantined, stopped-for-inspection). It holds no credential value, no environment variable value, no token, no session identifier, no owner identity, no executable path and no threshold number. Acquire and Release take an explicit time argument; the pool never reads a clock.
decisions.rationale: The operating shape is measured, not assumed: contracts/fixtures/valid/provider-standing-authorization.json authorizes codex, claude and opencode as one enum-constrained set, and the subscription is one identity per CLI, so there is exactly one slot per Provider and no rotation set to draw from. That makes the pool a selector over Providers, not over accounts of one Provider, and it makes the per-Provider concurrency ceiling one by construction rather than by policy -- two concurrent invocations on one subscription share one usage window, so a pool that handed out two slots would be lying about isolation. Excluding the credential is structural, not procedural: internal/runner.SecretBroker already owns per-Provider credential allowlisting and Grant.Apply is the only path that merges a value into an Invocation environment, so a pool field would be a second home for a value that already has exactly one. Excluding the executable path is the same argument: the approved provider-preflight record carries provider.executable_path bound by approval.subject_digest, and internal/runner.CostLedger.Reserve refuses when the resolved argv[0] disagrees, so a pool copy could silently diverge from the approved one. Naming the record by id rather than copying its limits is dp-v2-067 d6's ruling applied here. Taking time as an argument rather than storing a clock is what makes a cooldown deterministic and is what internal/domain's own real-clock scan requires of any package that must be reproducible.

decisions.decision: Provider quota in this task is a per-Provider usage window in internal/provider, and it is a different object from internal/quota and from internal/runner.CostLedger. It counts, per named window, only what the adapter layer can see: invocations attempted through this pool, and the token counts a Provider reported in Result.Usage, separating not-reported from zero. It carries a ceiling supplied by its caller and reports state from a closed set (within-window, exhausted, unknown). It contains no currency, no monetary amount, and no field or JSON key whose name contains usd, cost, price, billing, spend, budget or credit; a mechanical substring test over the emitted keys asserts that.
decisions.rationale: internal/quota is measured to be about something else entirely: its package comment, its Budget of 25000 reads / 10000 writes / 10000 deletes, its Counter with 32 accounting buckets, its StorageLevel and its ReadTransactionUsage are the Firestore daily free-tier reservation, and internal/application/ports.go imports it for ReserveQuota. Reusing that type for Provider usage would put two unrelated resources, with different units, different owners and different failure meanings, behind one name. CostLedger is also not this: it is runner-local, persisted to a file outside the repository at 0600, denominated in USD, bound to an owner-approved digest-bound record, fail-closed on Reserve and permanently halted above the 2.00 USD single-invocation anomaly threshold. docs/operations/provider-live-claude.md states its purpose plainly -- a runaway detector, never a billing rule -- and states its observation boundary: it records only invocations that passed through SupervisedInvocationRunner, so it cannot tell anyone the subscription's real remaining allowance and is not a substitute for the Provider's own usage display. The window therefore never decides whether a process may start (CostLedger alone has that authority, before exec) and never claims to know a subscription's remaining allowance; it is an input to breaker and pool selection only. The money-vocabulary ban is dp-v2-067 d6's substring rule applied one layer down: it is the only enforceable form of the standing authorization's own ruling that a threshold reached is a stop for inspection and never a billing event.

decisions.decision: internal/quota is not edited, and neither is internal/runner. Nothing in this task adds a field to, or reads a field from, either.
decisions.rationale: Two independent measured costs. First, ci/components.json assigns internal/quota/** to the roots of the infra component, whose reverse closure is eight components (api, application, control-plane, infra, reconciler, runner, store-firestore, store-memory) -- so a one-line edit there moves eight evidence keys and lands on the same application and store files the current serialization chain holds open. Second, and decisively, internal/quota/quota.go is a member of the published live exercise file set in .agents/v2/evidence/artifacts/V2-075-live-exercise-files.json, so editing it makes ev-v2-075-provider-live-claude-rebind's G6b intersection non-empty and forces a re-observation of the live claude exercise. internal/runner is excluded for the same G6b reason plus a substantive one: the per-Provider projection from a real CLI response to the parseable shape lives there and can only be written against a real response, which this task cannot obtain for codex or opencode. That projection work is V2-028's.

decisions.decision: The circuit breaker lives in internal/provider, is keyed by Provider name, and switches on internal/provider.FailureClass -- the package's own eight-value taxonomy, nine once V2-067 lands FailureUnauthenticated. internal/provider does not import internal/domain and gains no import at all, so the provider component stays a leaf in ci/components.json. The mapping from domain.FailureClass's seventeen values to breaker behaviour is recorded as a design table in this packet and in the runbook, as the Loop-level intent that V2-028 and the registry surface bind to; it is not encoded as an import.
decisions.rationale: The two taxonomies are already recorded as different, not duplicated: ev-v2-019-reconciler states that internal/provider's FailureClass is a separate taxonomy from domain's and not a duplicate of it. Importing internal/domain would create the first dependency edge out of the provider component and would require ci/components.json to change, which this task is forbidden to touch and which V2-045 owns. Keying the breaker on the class the adapter actually produces also keeps the decision where the observation is: the adapter is the only thing that saw the invocation, and translating to a Loop-level class before deciding would put a mapping between the observation and the decision for no gain.

decisions.decision: Which classes open the breaker, over domain.FailureClass's seventeen values. Opens on first occurrence: provider-quota (an explicit exhaustion signal needs no rate) and contract-incompatible (an output shape the adapter cannot parse will not parse on a retry). Counts toward a windowed count threshold: provider-transport (the ordinary provider-side fault, after the bounded retry failure-model.md section 2 already prescribes), and unknown at a strictly higher count than transport and never on a first occurrence. Opens only the narrower Provider-and-model circuit, leaving the Provider circuit closed: provider-model. Never opens the breaker, but moves the pool slot to a non-available state: secret-suspected (slot quarantined; clearing is a human act, never a probe), budget-exceeded (slot stopped-for-inspection), and provider-unauthenticated once V2-067 lands it (slot unauthenticated; the required action is the owner's, not a probe's). Never opens and never counts: invalid-input, policy-denied, capacity-unavailable, execution-lost, progress-stalled, verification-failed, external-ambiguous, integration-conflict, preview-regression, promotion-partial. The provider-local classes timeout and cancelled map as: timeout counts toward the transport threshold and marks any resulting open as ambiguous; cancelled never counts.
decisions.rationale: Each row follows a measured rule rather than taste. docs/architecture/failure-model.md section 4 says to open on failure rate or an explicit quota signal, which fixes provider-quota as immediate and provider-transport as rate-based. Its section 2 assigns provider-model the action evaluate compatible model candidates in the same pool, which is impossible if the whole Provider is open, so the circuit must be the narrower one. Its section 2 assigns secret-suspected the actions stop, redact, revoke, and section 4's last line forbids treating a permanent authentication or permission failure as a transient retry -- so neither can be a state a timed probe leaves. budget-exceeded is excluded on the ruling docs/operations/provider-live-claude.md already makes about its own thresholds: reaching one is a stop for inspection, neither a success nor a failure, so a breaker that opened on it would report a Provider fault for a Loop-side stop. The eight non-counting classes are excluded because none of them is an observation about the Provider: invalid-input and policy-denied are about our request, execution-lost and progress-stalled are about the Runner or the lease, verification-failed means the Provider worked and the change was wrong, and external-ambiguous, integration-conflict, preview-regression and promotion-partial happen after the invocation ended. progress-stalled deserves its own note because it is the tempting one: failure-model.md section 2 routes it to checkpoint, TERM/KILL and a new Execution, and section 5 insists on distinguishing the process is certainly gone from the result cannot be established, so opening a circuit on an ambiguity that does not name the Provider would take a working Provider out of service on evidence about something else. timeout counts but marks the open ambiguous for the same reason section 6 gives: a timeout is not a failure, it is an unknown result.

decisions.decision: Closing is never a function of elapsed time alone. open to half-open requires all of: the cooldown deadline has passed under the clock the caller passes in; the pool issues exactly one probe token and no second token exists while one is outstanding; and, when the opening class was provider-quota, the usage window has rolled over -- elapsed time alone does not make an exhausted window fresh. half-open to closed requires a reported successful invocation observation, not the issuance of the probe. half-open back to open on a failed probe multiplies the cooldown up to a declared ceiling and does not reset the counter. For contract-incompatible no probe is ever eligible: closing requires an explicitly observed change of declared CLI version. For quarantined and stopped-for-inspection there is no probe and no timer at all; only an explicit external clearance moves the slot.
decisions.rationale: failure-model.md section 4 already prescribes reset time or a bounded probe, exactly one probe, close on success and increase cooldown on failure; this decision only makes the two non-time conditions explicit, because a time-only close is what turns a breaker into a retry loop with extra steps -- and against a Provider whose usage window has not rolled over, a timed probe is a guaranteed second exhaustion that consumes a real invocation. Requiring an injected clock is not a preference: the acceptance forbids fixed sleeps, timers and goroutines, and a breaker that read time.Now would be untestable without one of them. Refusing a probe for contract-incompatible follows from what the class means -- the adapter and the CLI disagree about the output shape, and nothing about waiting changes either side's version.

decisions.decision: An open breaker is stated as a decision of this Loop, not as a condition of the Provider. The exported state names the Loop's action (the closed set is sending, not-sending, probing) and every not-sending value carries the closed set of failure classes that produced it, the window the count was taken over, and an observation_scope value stating that only invocations that passed through this Loop's own execution path were counted. No identifier anywhere in the breaker, the pool or the window is named healthy, unhealthy, broken, down, up, alive, dead or ok, and a mechanical name scan asserts that.
decisions.rationale: The counted population is measured to be a strict subset of reality. docs/operations/provider-live-claude.md's observation-boundary section records that the ledger sees only invocations that went through SupervisedInvocationRunner, and gives the measured example: six real claude invocations run by hand from a shell during V2-017 appear nowhere in it. A breaker built on that same population therefore knows how this Loop's own calls went and nothing about the Provider's condition, so a field named healthy would be false in the only case that matters -- a Provider a human is using successfully while the Loop's own last three attempts failed. dp-v2-067 d5 already separated stopped-for-inspection from unavailable for the same reason and refused to infer health from silence; this is the same refusal one layer down, and the name scan is the only durable form of it.

decisions.decision: PrepareHandoff already exists in internal/provider/handoff.go and is exercised by one existing assertion inside TestFailureClassificationAndHandoff. It is kept and extended, not replaced. Added: Handoff.Validate; a canonical content digest over the packet's carried facts (IncrementID, Constraints, Decisions, Artifacts, Verification, Unresolved) recorded on the Handoff and re-checked when it is converted back; RequestFromHandoff, which turns a Handoff into a Request for the target adapter and refuses when the target is not one of the three names, when the recomputed content digest disagrees, or when the target's breaker is not sending; and a bounded, closed-enum-only attempt history (from, to, failure class) with no free text, which lets a second handoff refuse to hand back to a Provider already tried for the same Increment.
decisions.rationale: The measured gap is that today nothing converts a Handoff back into anything, so the type records an intention that no code consumes and no test can catch losing. The content digest is what turns Increment, Artifact and Evidence preservation from a property nobody checks into a fail-closed one: a handoff that drops an Artifact currently produces a valid Handoff, and after the change it produces a refusal. The history exists because failure-model.md section 3 counts the same failure fingerprint and the same approach as retry-budget dimensions, and a handoff chain with no memory is exactly how a Loop ping-pongs A to B to A while both budgets read as untouched. Everything added is a pure function over values already in the packet, so internal/provider gains no import and stays a leaf.

decisions.decision: Attribution of M6's four completion conditions. Condition 1 (confirm each Provider's success, error, quota and cancel against the real thing) is wholly V2-028; V2-027 satisfies no part of it. Condition 2 (demonstrate a shared adapter change across all three Providers) is split: V2-027 supplies the contract-fixture layer, one table over three adapter values, and V2-028 owns the demonstration the condition asks for, because validation.md puts a shared adapter change across three Providers under Preview capability exercise. Condition 3 (do not lose Increment, Artifact or Evidence after a Provider change) is split: V2-027 proves fixture-level preservation and fail-closed refusal on loss, and V2-028 proves preservation through a real switch with a real journal, lease, Increment and Evidence record. Condition 4 (opencode does not cross the shared sandbox boundary) is wholly V2-028; V2-027 can show only that OpenCodeAdapter.Build cannot ask to leave -- WorkingDirectory pinned to the workspace, argv free of injection and traversal, environment set-equal to the approved base names -- which is a property of the request, not of the process.
decisions.rationale: The split is derived mechanically from where each condition's witness has to run. Gate rule G3.1 restricts a condition naming a real Provider CLI to live evidence carrying the CLI version and machine identifier, and G3.3 refuses unit, fake, stub and contract-test evidence at every grade, which settles conditions 1 and 4 outright. Condition 4 is worth stating carefully rather than briefly: validation.md proves workspace confinement with a rootless user and mount namespace against a real process on a real kernel, with a positive control showing the write succeeds without the namespace, and none of that is reachable from a fixture. Condition 3 splits because the packet-level half is a pure-value property and the continuity half needs a journal, a lease and a fencing token, which live in internal/runner and which this task does not touch.

decisions.decision: internal/domain is not edited and no FailureClass constant is added to it. The seventeen values are sufficient for the table in d12, and the one new class this area needs -- an unauthenticated Provider -- is already assigned to V2-067 as internal/provider.FailureUnauthenticated by dp-v2-067 d9.
decisions.rationale: The V2-049 precedent is what argues against an addition here, not for one. V2-049 added promotion-partial, secret-suspected and contract-incompatible to close a measured drift: ev-v2-019-reconciler had recorded that docs/architecture/failure-model.md's taxonomy table listed seventeen classes while domain declared fourteen, and exactly those three had no constant. That is an addition that removed a divergence between a document and the code. This task has no such divergence to close: every class d12's table needs already exists, the table is a mapping and not a new class, and adding a domain constant would put a value in the one package whose closure the M1 gate proved, for a decision that happens in a leaf package that does not import it.

decisions.decision: Editing internal/provider makes ev-v2-075-provider-live-claude-rebind's G6b intersection non-empty, and V2-027 neither hides that nor tries to repair it. The evidence records the measured intersection, states that internal/provider/adapters.go, provider.go and handoff.go are members of the published exercise file set, and names V2-028 as the owner of the re-observation. V2-027 does not touch .agents/v2/provider-preflight/**, does not re-run any live suite, and does not adjust any threshold.
decisions.rationale: The set is published and checkable: .agents/v2/evidence/artifacts/V2-075-live-exercise-files.json lists 76 paths and all three internal/provider source files are among them, so any edit to the package produces a non-empty intersection and G6b requires a re-observation regardless of the reason. Repairing it here is impossible and would be harmful to attempt: docs/operations/provider-live-claude.md records that V2-075's ledger was consumed to 12 of 12 and instructs the next runner of the live suite not to raise the thresholds but to obtain a new owner-approved record with a new ledger path -- an owner action. It is also unnecessary: V2-028 re-observes all three real CLIs, claude included, and will need a fresh record and ledger of its own for exactly the reason the runbook gives, so the re-observation this task invalidates is one V2-028 was always going to perform.

decisions.decision: Component evidence keys. The reverse closure of a change to internal/provider/** is six components -- provider, runner, reconciler, api, control-plane, store-firestore -- and editing docs/** and .agents/** additionally moves docs and task-ledger. One evidence record is issued, for the component provider. The other seven key movements are recorded as a measured note under gate rule G6a, naming the argv that measured them, and no second evidence record is created for a component this task did not verify.
decisions.rationale: The closure is computed from ci/components.json, not guessed: runner declares provider as a dependency, reconciler declares it as a verification dependency, api, control-plane and store-firestore each reach it through runner. That reproduces V2-071's measurement (touching internal/runner moved api and store-firestore) and extends it by one hop. Issuing one record follows the same rule V2-019 followed when it recorded a19-staleness-note rather than minting records for components it had not verified; and G6a is now the applicable freshness rule for everything make check re-runs, which is all six of these.

decisions.decision: V2-027 enters the serialization chain immediately after V2-067, giving V2-069 to V2-067 to V2-027 to V2-073 to V2-068 to V2-065 to V2-072. Two independent collisions force it: V2-067's allowed_paths include internal/provider/provider.go, internal/provider/adapters.go and internal/provider/provider_test.go, the same three files this task restructures; and .agents/v2/evidence/index.json is in every chain task's allowed_paths, so no task in the chain can append to the ledger concurrently with another. Ordering after rather than before V2-067 is deliberate.
decisions.rationale: The direction matters because the two tasks are not symmetric. V2-067's provider change is small and additive -- one FailureClass constant, one branch in normalize, two assertions -- and dp-v2-027 d12's table needs a row for that constant, which it can only write against a constant that exists. Landing V2-027 first would force V2-067's work order to be amended to cover a table it never saw, and would make V2-067 rebase onto a restructured adapters.go. The reverse rebase is a two-line replay. Note for the coordinator: apart from those three files and the evidence index, V2-027 shares no path with any chain member -- it touches no api handler, no application port, service or read model, no openapi document, no owner console and neither store -- so if the ledger append is serialized by another mechanism, the only hard edge is V2-067 to V2-027.

risks: The opencode and codex flag surfaces are read from --help, not from a completed run, so a flag that help declares may still behave differently in practice. That residual is real and is not closed here; it is closed by V2-028's first real invocation of each CLI. The mitigation is that the adapter declares only flags help declares, so the failure mode moves from an unmeasured claim to a measured one.

The nine-case matrix over three adapters plus the pool, window, breaker and handoff seams is a large test surface in one package, and internal/provider currently has 3 top-level tests. A matrix written as three copies rather than one table would satisfy every assertion while defeating the purpose of the matrix, which is that a change to shared code reaches all three. The acceptance therefore requires one table driven over adapter values, and requires reporting how many distinct table drivers exist.

Editing internal/provider forces a live re-observation of the claude exercise (d18) whose ledger is exhausted, so between V2-027 landing and V2-028 running, no live provider evidence in the repository satisfies G6b. Any gate judged in that window must treat provider-live-claude as requiring re-observation. This is stated rather than mitigated, because the alternative is to not complete the adapters.

The breaker's population is only what this Loop invoked (d14), so its state can disagree with a Provider that a human is using successfully. If a reader takes not-sending as the Provider is broken, the surface has traded one wrong reading for another. The mitigation is the state naming and the observation_scope field, plus the runbook saying so in words.

The pool's one-slot-per-Provider shape is correct for the measured subscription set (one identity per CLI) and would be wrong if a second account of the same CLI ever appeared. That consequence is recorded rather than pre-built: a speculative account discriminator now would put owner identity into a record this design keeps free of it, and dp-v2-067 d2 already made the same call for the registry key.
